papers.title: Public R&D and the Automation of Manufacturing: Evidence from the Space Race
papers.abstract: This paper examines how public research and development shaped the direction of technological change during the Cold War–era Space Race and its consequences for US manufacturing. While prior research has documented the effects of public R&D on innovation and economic growth, less is known about whether mission-oriented public investment directed innovation toward automation and how this affected labor markets. We exploit variation in exposure to NASA's Space Race investments across industries and locations to estimate the effects of public R&D on innovation and manufacturing outcomes from 1947 to 1992. Combining newly developed measures of automation in full-text patent data with historical evidence on government involvement in patenting, we show that NASA-sponsored patents are systematically more automation-intensive than non-NASA patents within the same technological classes. Industries and locations more exposed to Space Race activity experienced persistent declines in labor share, consistent with the diffusion of labor-saving technologies developed for space applications. In contrast, we find little evidence of systematic changes in skill composition. These findings show that mission-oriented public R&D can shape the direction of technological change and have lasting distributional consequences.

papers.title: A Beckerian Theory of Taxation
papers.abstract: We study taxation in matching environments in which both equilibrium sorting and the sharing of match surplus are endogenous. Tax reforms lead to complex adjustments in sorting and surplus sharing patterns across the whole economy. We develop a general approach for characterizing these equilibrium adjustments using matching elasticities, which are primitive objects that describe how agents' matching choices are affected by pecuniary payoffs in partial equilibrium. Applying this approach to a workhorse model of family formation, we first show that the sorting and surplus sharing responses are closely linked to complementarities in the creation of economic surplus, as first emphasized by Becker (1973). We then describe the effects of arbitrary tax reforms on tax revenues, the utilities of different agents, and social welfare; design tests to assess Pareto efficiency of existing tax systems; derive formulas that characterize optimal taxes; and propose numerical techniques to compute them. In a calibrated model, we find that optimal marginal tax rates are substantially lower and less progressive than in the Mirrleesian benchmark.

papers.title: Coase Meets Negishi: Property Rights, Welfare Weights, and Distributional Consequences in Climate Economics
papers.abstract: We develop a property-rights based approach for defining welfare weights in economic models of climate change. Whether there is a "right to pollute" or a "right to no pollution" is increasingly contested in legislatures, courts, and international climate negotiations. We show how these notions of property rights can provide the basis for "Coasean welfare weights" that are applicable in multilateral public goods settings. Distributional questions are addressed through positive analysis, conditional on property rights, rather than normative views about redistribution. The implied transfers are consistent with a bargained solution over the net benefits of addressing climate change and reflect the value of property rights over emissions. The approach defines efficient allocations that generate Pareto improvements, in contrast to commonly used Negishi weights. We implement the approach in a global integrated assessment model to quantify what countries have at stake in ongoing political and legal debates about emissions-related property rights.

papers.title: Governance Regimes, Economic Mobility, and the Composition of Public Investment: Evidence from the Democratization of Villages in India
papers.abstract: We develop a quantifiable general-equilibrium model of village governance, motivated by India’s democratization, to study how political institutions shape public goods provision and economic development. The model features two groups, landowners and landless workers, with different preferences over public goods such as irrigation, schools, and employment programs. Households from both groups can enter nonfarm entrepreneurship, but face credit-dependent entry costs. We compare oligarchy, where landowners control public goods decisions, with democracy, where electoral competition determines policy based on the relative sizes of the two groups. The calibrated model predicts that democratization’s effects on public goods and growth are not uniform; they depend on population composition and the ease of occupational mobility through access to credit. Using a 37-year village-level panel from India (1971–2006) and exploiting variation in democratization driven by state and national reforms, we find strong support for these predictions. Financial intermediation shifts landless households’ preferences from wage-enhancing policies toward schooling, increasing nonfarm business entry. As a result, democracy provides fewer schools than oligarchy when credit is unavailable, but more schools when credit is accessible. We also show that transfers to the landless increase schooling under democracy but reduce it under oligarchy. These findings highlight how governance structures and economic conditions jointly determine the effectiveness of development policies.
